doc_access_review_q3.title: Q3 2026 Access Review Report
doc_access_review_q3.content:
# Q3 2026 Access Review

**Author:** Ananya Iyer · **Scope:** Production systems, repositories, cloud accounts
**Cadence:** Quarterly (Security Policy v2.1)

## Method

Reviewed every human principal with production access against their current team and project
assignment. Repository access was reconciled from the identity provider against team membership in
the company directory.

## Findings

| # | Finding | Severity | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Two former contractors retained AWS console access | High | Revoked |
| 2 | Atlas production database access granted to a rotated-off engineer | Medium | Revoked |
| 3 | Shared service account used interactively by three engineers | High | Rotated, per-user creds issued |
| 4 | Audit trail for one legacy session service incomplete | Medium | Open — superseded by ADR-025 |
| 5 | Repository admin rights on 3 orgs wider than policy allows | Low | Remaining 2 owners confirmed |

14 of 16 findings closed; 2 remain open and are tracked to Orion sign-in rework.

## Recommendation

Finding 4 is structural, not a process lapse: the legacy session service did not log token events.
Rather than patch it, complete ADR-025 so all sessions are issued and logged by the Orion gateway.
This is the strongest evidence in favour of the central gateway and is referenced in the ADR-025
supporting material.

## Follow-up

- Q4 review scheduled for 2026-12-30.
- Per-workload service accounts migrating to short-lived credentials via the gateway.
- Customer PII reads added to the audit trail under ATLAS-110.

doc_api_docs_atlas.title: Atlas Reports API Documentation
doc_api_docs_atlas.content:
# Atlas Reports API

Base URL: `https://atlas.novatech.example/api/v2`

All endpoints require a bearer token issued by the Auth Gateway and an `X-Purpose` header
describing the business purpose of the request (required for PII audit logging per ATLAS-110).

## GET /reports/usage

Returns usage aggregates for the caller's tenant.

**Query parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `from` | date | Inclusive period start |
| `to` | date | Inclusive period end |
| `plan` | string | Optional plan filter |
| `region` | string | Optional region filter |
| `group_by` | string | `day`, `week` or `month` |

**Response**

```json
{
  "tenant_id": "t_8421",
  "period": {"from": "2026-09-01", "to": "2026-09-30"},
  "reports": [
    {"bucket": "2026-09-01", "sum": 18402, "unit": "api_calls", "plan": "scale"}
  ],
  "staleness_seconds": 42
}
```

The response is served from the read replica; `staleness_seconds` tells the client how far behind
the replica is so the UI can show a freshness badge.

## GET /customers/{id}

Returns the customer record with plan and region. Sensitive fields are redacted unless the caller
carries the `customer:pii` scope.

## Error codes

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 401 | Missing or invalid token |
| 403 | Missing scope |
| 409 | Schema version mismatch (see ATLAS-107) |
| 429 | Rate limited, retry after `Retry-After` |
| 503 | Replica unavailable, retry with backoff |

## Notes for consumers

Mercury consumes `/reports/usage` and must tolerate `staleness_seconds` up to 120 before alerting.
The `sum` field name is stable since v2.8 (contract drift fixed under MERCURY-304).

doc_atlas_migration_design.title: Atlas Database Migration Design
doc_atlas_migration_design.content:
# Atlas Database Migration Design (MongoDB to PostgreSQL)

## Purpose

This document is the supporting design for ADR-018, which moved Atlas from MongoDB to PostgreSQL.

## Problem statement

Three forces drove the migration:

1. **Consistency.** Reporting aggregates built in application code disagreed with operational
   counts under concurrent writes. MongoDB multi-document transactions existed but were slow and
   rarely used by the legacy repository layer.
2. **Join cost.** Cohort reporting needs joins across customers, plans and usage. Stitching in
   application code made every report a bespoke query.
3. **Cost.** Managed MongoDB spend grew 3.4x year over year while our Postgres footprint stayed flat.

## Target design

PostgreSQL 16 on AWS RDS with multi-AZ. Monthly partitioned `usage_events`, encrypted PII columns,
PgBouncer for pooling, and a read replica for reporting (ADR-020).

## Migration strategy

Three phases:

- **Phase 1 — Dual write.** Writes go to MongoDB first, then PostgreSQL, with divergence logging (ATLAS-101).
- **Phase 2 — Shadow reads.** Reads still served by MongoDB while PostgreSQL responses are compared (ATLAS-101).
- **Phase 3 — Cutover and decommission.** Reads flip to PostgreSQL, then MongoDB is retired (ATLAS-106).

Backfill runs in resumable 50k-row chunks to keep replica lag under two seconds (ATLAS-102).
Index tuning for customer-by-region and customer-by-plan lookups landed in ATLAS-104.

## Rollback

If divergence exceeds 0.1% of sampled queries, reads revert to MongoDB for one release cycle.

## Decision context

Reviewed with Priya Sharma and Meera Krishnan, approved by David Wilson in the Database
Architecture Review meeting on 2026-08-12 (ADR-018).

doc_data_pipeline_design.title: Atlas Ingestion Pipeline Design
doc_data_pipeline_design.content:
# Atlas Ingestion Pipeline Design

**Author:** Meera Krishnan · **Owner:** Arun Kumar · **Related:** ADR-018, ATLAS-102, ATLAS-107

## Overview

The ingestion pipeline turns raw product API events into the canonical `usage_events` table that
powers reporting and billing.

## Stages

1. **Collect.** FastAPI ingest endpoints accept batched events, validate against the event schema
   and write to a Redis stream.
2. **Normalise.** Workers consume the stream, coerce types, resolve tenant and plan identifiers,
   and emit normalised rows.
3. **Load.** Rows are written to PostgreSQL in 5k-row transactions with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`
   for idempotency.
4. **Aggregate.** Hourly materialised views roll usage up by tenant, plan and region.

## Backfill

Historical backfill from MongoDB runs in resumable 50k-row chunks with checkpoints in Redis. Chunk
size was chosen so replica lag stays under two seconds, which is the threshold the reporting
staleness badge tolerates (ATLAS-102).

## Data quality

- Event schema version is enforced at ingest; unknown versions are rejected with a metric.
- A nightly reconciliation job compares hourly aggregates against raw counts and alerts on
  divergence above 0.05%.
- Contract tests compare ingest output to the API model, added after ATLAS-107 found a
  `plan_tier` vs `planTier` mismatch.

## Failure modes

| Failure | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Redis stream full | Ingest sheds load with 429 and a retry hint |
| Postgres primary failover | Workers retry with exponential backoff, stream retains events |
| Schema drift | Rows quarantined to `usage_events_quarantine` and alerted |

## Open work

Cold-data archival to S3 (ATLAS-108) and a schema registry to remove the manual contract tests.

doc_atlas_status_report.content:
# Project Atlas — Q3 2026 Status Report

**Overall health:** At risk (yellow)
**Owner:** Arun Kumar · **Lead:** David Wilson · **Product:** Sarah Thomas

## Summary

The PostgreSQL migration is functionally complete for new writes and backfill is 92% done. The
project is flagged at risk for schedule, not for correctness: reporting latency and connection
pooling both need work before we can decommission MongoDB.

## Progress this quarter

- ADR-018 approved and implemented for primary workloads.
- ADR-020 approved: read replica added for reporting.
- ATLAS-102 backfill at 92% of historical usage events.
- ATLAS-104 index tuning closed with a 6x improvement on customer lookups.

## Risks

1. **Connection pool exhaustion (ATLAS-109).** PgBouncer saturates at 600 RPS in load tests.
   Mitigation under investigation by Arun with Vikram's load harness.
2. **Reporting latency (ATLAS-105).** Dashboard p95 hit 2.8s during ingest peaks. The read replica
   work moves reporting off the primary.
3. **Schema drift (ATLAS-107).** Ingest and API disagree on `planTier` casing; a contract test is
   being added.

## Next quarter

- Finish backfill and shadow-read validation, then retire MongoDB (ATLAS-106).
- Complete audit logging for PII reads (ATLAS-110) ahead of the security review.
- Hand stable reporting views to the Mercury beta.

## Budget note

Infrastructure spend is down 19% quarter over quarter, driven by the MongoDB reduction. No new
headcount requested.

doc_atlas_architecture.title: Atlas System Architecture
doc_atlas_architecture.content:
# Atlas System Architecture

## Overview

Atlas is NovaTech's customer data platform. It ingests product usage events, joins them with
customer records, and serves analytics to the Mercury dashboard and the Nova knowledge pipeline.

## Current topology

Ingestion workers consume events from the product APIs and write them through a FastAPI ingest
service. Since ADR-018 the system of record is PostgreSQL on AWS RDS, with MongoDB retained only
as a shadow source during the cutover window. Reporting queries run against a PostgreSQL read
replica as approved in ADR-020.

Redis provides the result cache for dashboard aggregates and the durable queue for background
ingest jobs. All services run as containers on AWS EKS (ADR-021) and are deployed through GitHub
Actions pipelines with required checks on main.

## Data model core

Three tables carry most of the load: `customers`, `usage_events` and `plans`. Usage events are
append-only and partitioned monthly. Customer PII columns are encrypted at rest and every read is
audit logged per ATLAS-110.

## Why relational

The reporting use cases are dominated by joins between customers, plans and usage aggregates.
Application-side stitching in the MongoDB era produced inconsistent aggregates and cost 3.4x more
to operate. PostgreSQL gives transactional consistency, window functions for cohort queries, and a
single operational model shared with Orion and Nova.

## Known pressure points

- Connection pooling saturates near 600 RPS (ATLAS-109).
- Reporting latency regressed during write peaks, tracked by ADR-020 and ATLAS-105.
- Dual-write divergence checks are still running (ATLAS-101).

## Owners

Arun Kumar is the technical owner. Meera Krishnan owns the ingestion pipeline. David Wilson
approved the architecture. Sarah Thomas owns the product-facing reporting commitments.

doc_frontend_design_system.title: NovaTech Design System Notes
doc_frontend_design_system.content:
# NovaTech Design System Notes

**Owner:** Rahul Menon · **Consumers:** Mercury, Nova dashboard, internal tools

## Principles

1. **Information before decoration.** Every pixel either carries meaning or gets removed.
2. **Dark first.** The default theme is dark; light mode is a supported alternative, not an
   afterthought.
3. **Motion with purpose.** Transitions explain state changes, never entertain.

## Foundations

- **Colour:** deep slate surfaces (`#0f1218`, `#161b24`), one accent (cyan `#38bdf8`), semantic
  colours for success, warning and danger. Contrast checked against WCAG AA in both themes.
- **Typography:** system UI stack for product pages; monospace for identifiers, ticket keys and
  code. Numeric data uses tabular figures.
- **Spacing:** 4px base scale. Cards use 16px padding, 12px gaps.
- **Elevation:** two levels only — resting and raised. Raised surfaces get a 1px border plus a soft
  shadow; we avoid large blur radii.

## Components

Buttons (primary, ghost, danger), inputs with inline validation, cards, badges for status
(`healthy`, `degraded`, `blocked`), and a data table with virtualised rows. Status colours are
always paired with a text label; colour alone never conveys state.

## Charts

Axis and grid lines at 12% opacity. Legends use the accessibility palette and sit above the chart
on narrow viewports. Tooltips show exact values, never rounded ones.

## Accessibility

Keyboard reachable controls, visible focus rings, `prefers-reduced-motion` respected. Icons that
carry meaning have text labels.

## Implementation notes

Tokens ship as CSS custom properties plus a TypeScript object. Components are themed by token, never
by conditional classes. New components require a story and an axe check before merge.

doc_engineering_guidelines.title: NovaTech Engineering Guidelines v3
doc_engineering_guidelines.content:
# NovaTech Engineering Guidelines v3

These guidelines are the default for every repository. Deviations require an ADR.

## Language and framework defaults

- **Backend:** Python 3.12 with FastAPI (ADR-009). Typed Pydantic request/response models and a
  generated OpenAPI schema are mandatory for every service.
- **Frontend:** React with Vite and TypeScript (ADR-012). Shared components live in the internal
  design system.
- **Ephemeral state:** Redis for caches, sessions and queues (ADR-006).
- **Graph and relationship data:** FalkorDB with parameterised Cypher (ADR-015).

## Data

PostgreSQL is the system of record (ADR-018). Schema changes ship as versioned migrations and are
reviewed by a second engineer. No service writes to another service's tables; use its API.

## Delivery

- Trunk-based development, short-lived branches, required checks on main (ADR-017).
- Every change to production infrastructure goes through GitOps; no manual deploys (ADR-021).
- Tests required for new behaviour: unit tests for logic, API tests for endpoints, an integration
  test for anything touching two services.

## Observability

Structured JSON logs with correlation IDs, RED metrics for every service, and dashboards that
answer "is the customer affected" before "which box is hot".

## Code review

Reviewers check for: typed interfaces at boundaries, explicit error handling, no secrets in the
repo, and documentation for any non-obvious decision. Reviews are about the code, never the
person who wrote it.

## AI features

Any AI feature must (1) cite its sources, (2) degrade gracefully when a model provider is
unavailable, and (3) require human confirmation before performing write actions. Prompt and
evaluation changes are reviewed like code.

doc_onboarding_handbook.title: Engineering Onboarding Handbook
doc_onboarding_handbook.content:
# Engineering Onboarding Handbook

Welcome to NovaTech. This handbook gets you from laptop to first pull request in a day.

## Week one

1. **Accounts.** SSO through the identity provider, then ask your team lead for repository access.
2. **Local environment.** Docker Desktop, Python 3.12, Node 20, and `uv` or `poetry`. Every service
   has a `docker compose` file that boots it with dependencies.
3. **Read these first.** Engineering Guidelines v3, the Security Policy, and the architecture
   document for the project you joined.

## How we work

We develop in trunk-based style with short-lived branches and required checks on main. Every
change needs one review. We use ADRs for decisions that are expensive to reverse: if you are
choosing a database, an auth model, or a deployment platform, write an ADR.

## Who to ask

- Backend, data platform, database migrations: **Arun Kumar**
- AI platform, agent orchestration, retrieval quality: **Priya Sharma**
- Frontend, design system, performance: **Rahul Menon**
- Kubernetes, CI/CD, cloud cost: **Vikram Raj**
- Security reviews, threat modelling, access: **Ananya Iyer**
- Data pipelines and warehouse modelling: **Meera Krishnan**
- Roadmap, priorities, customer context: **Sarah Thomas**
- Architecture escalations: **David Wilson**

## Your first task

Pick a "good first issue" from your team's backlog. Your mentor reviews it with you. Team leads own
the backlog grooming, so ask them if the issue is unclear.

## Where knowledge lives

Documents, decisions and meeting notes are indexed in the company knowledge graph. Ask Nova in the
dashboard: it answers with sources, and walking the virtual office to a desk or room gives you the
same graph with context.

doc_incident_2026_06_21.title: Incident Report INC-042 — Failed Production Deploy
doc_incident_2026_06_21.content:
# INC-042 — Failed Production Deploy (2026-06-21)

**Severity:** 2 · **Duration:** 74 minutes · **Author:** Vikram Raj

## Summary

A production deploy of the Atlas ingest service left the fleet in a mixed state: six of nine EC2
instances ran the new build while three kept the old one. Ingest throughput dropped 40% and
duplicate usage rows appeared for 11 minutes.

## Timeline

- 14:02 — Deploy command issued by hand over SSH to the instance list.
- 14:05 — Three instances rejected the artifact due to a checksum mismatch.
- 14:09 — Mixed-version fleet caused duplicate writes for tenants on both versions.
- 15:16 — Fleet rolled back to the previous artifact; duplication stopped.

## Root cause

Deploys were a hand-rolled script over a hard-coded instance list with no atomicity, no
verification and no rollback path. The checksum mismatch was a symptom; the absence of a release
mechanism was the cause.

## Impact

11 minutes of duplicate usage rows (since deduplicated), 40% ingest degradation for 74 minutes, no
customer data loss.

## Contributing factors

- No staging environment matched production at the time.
- Artifact checksums were computed per host rather than centrally.

## Actions taken

1. Approved ADR-021: move production to AWS EKS with GitOps deployments (approved 2026-07-09).
2. Added artifact checksum verification to the release pipeline.
3. Staging cluster raised to production parity in node count.

## Lessons

Deployment is a system, not a command. Standardise the platform before optimising the process.
This incident is the primary evidence behind ADR-021.

doc_incident_inc_047.title: Incident Report INC-047 — AI Gateway Latency Regression
doc_incident_inc_047.content:
# INC-047 — AI Gateway Latency Regression (2026-09-22)

**Severity:** 3 · **Duration:** 6 days (regression, not outage) · **Author:** Vikram Raj

## Summary

After the September cache redesign, AI Services p99 latency rose from 1.9s to 4.7s. No requests
failed, but interactive Nova sessions felt sluggish and the team's own usage dropped.

## Timeline

- Sep 16 — Cache redesign deployed, moving all workloads onto one Redis keyspace.
- Sep 18 — AI gateway p99 crosses 3s; alert threshold not yet breached.
- Sep 22 — Weekly incident triage (meet_012) confirms the correlation.
- Sep 26 — Dedicated Redis namespace for AI workloads restores p99 to 2.0s.

## Root cause

The shared Redis keyspace let high-churn report caches evict the AI gateway's prompt-cache entries
under `allkeys-lru`. Eviction churn increased upstream model calls, which dominate latency.

## Impact

Elevated latency for six days. No data loss, no failed requests, no customer-visible errors.

## Actions taken

- Dedicated Redis namespace per workload class.
- Cache hit ratio dashboard added; alert at below 60% for AI workloads.
- NOVA-205 tracks the permanent fix and verification.

## Lessons

Caching is a shared resource with a fairness problem. Per-workload isolation should have been part
of the cache redesign review. Triage cadence caught this, but two days later than an alert would
have.

doc_meeting_db_architecture_2026_08_12.title: Meeting Notes — Database Architecture Review (2026-08-12)
doc_meeting_db_architecture_2026_08_12.content:
# Database Architecture Review — 2026-08-12

**Attendees:** Arun Kumar, Priya Sharma, David Wilson, Meera Krishnan
**Outcome:** ADR-018 approved

## Agenda

1. MongoDB to PostgreSQL migration proposal for Atlas
2. Reporting join strategy
3. Cutover phasing and rollback criteria

## Discussion

Arun presented the cost and consistency analysis: MongoDB spend had grown 3.4x year over year,
and reporting aggregates built in application code disagreed with operational counts under
concurrent writes. Meera showed that cohort reporting requires joins across customers, plans and
usage events, which the document store could not express efficiently.

Priya confirmed that Nova ingestion also needs relational guarantees: the knowledge graph seed
pipeline reads canonical project and decision data, and inconsistent aggregates would poison
retrieval quality. She supported PostgreSQL as the system of record.

David asked about rollback. Arun described the three-phase plan with divergence logging at 0.1%
threshold from the migration design document. David approved ADR-018 with that rollback clause.

## Decisions

- **ADR-018 approved:** move Atlas from MongoDB to PostgreSQL on AWS RDS.
- Dual-write shadow reads proceed under ATLAS-101.
- Backfill sized at 50k-row resumable chunks (ATLAS-102).

## Actions

| Action | Owner | Due |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dual-write divergence logging | Arun Kumar | 2026-08-22 |
| Backfill scripts with checkpoints | Meera Krishnan | 2026-08-29 |
| Reporting view rewrite | Arun Kumar | 2026-09-12 |

doc_mercury_frontend_architecture.title: Mercury Frontend Architecture
doc_mercury_frontend_architecture.content:
# Mercury Frontend Architecture

**Author:** Rahul Menon · **Stack:** React 18, Vite, TypeScript (ADR-012)

## Structure

Feature-sliced layout: `features/reports`, `features/account`, `features/shared`. Each feature owns
its components, hooks and API client. Cross-feature imports go through the shared design system,
never sideways into another feature.

## Data layer

A thin typed client wraps the Atlas Reports API. Response types are generated from the OpenAPI
schema so contract drift fails at compile time — the same class of bug as MERCURY-304 but caught in
CI instead of production.

Caching uses stale-while-revalidate: the dashboard renders cached data with a freshness badge while
refetching. The freshness badge reads `staleness_seconds` from the API, tolerating up to 120s before
warning.

## Rendering performance

The usage table is windowed and virtualised (MERCURY-302). Above 10k rows we render only visible
rows plus a 20-row overscan; sorting and filtering are memoised over a normalised index.

Charts render to canvas with a shared theme object. Legend colours come from the accessibility-safe
palette; ADR for dark mode contrast is tracked in MERCURY-303.

## State

Server state lives in the query cache; UI state lives in local component state. There is no global
store, deliberately: the dashboard has no cross-feature client state worth centralising.

## Testing

Vitest for units, Playwright for the three critical journeys (login, view report, export CSV).
Accessibility checked with axe on every component story.

## Known debt

Charts re-render on window resize without debounce, and the export path duplicates formatting
logic that lives in the shared package.

doc_mercury_requirements.title: Mercury Product Requirements Document
doc_mercury_requirements.content:
# Mercury — Product Requirements Document

**Owner:** Sarah Thomas · **Engineering owner:** Rahul Menon · **Status:** In development

## Problem

Customers see their NovaTech usage only through monthly emailed PDFs. Support tickets about
"missing usage" average 40 per month, and the top churn reason in exit interviews is "we cannot
see what we are paying for".

## Goals

1. Give customers a self-serve, role-aware usage dashboard.
2. Cut "missing usage" tickets by 60% within two quarters.
3. Ship on the standard React, Vite and TypeScript stack (ADR-012).

## Requirements

- **R1 — Reports:** usage by plan, region and period with CSV export. Data from the Atlas reports
  API, served from the PostgreSQL read replica (ADR-020).
- **R2 — Roles:** report tabs are gated by the Orion role claim; the frontend must not decide
  authorization on its own.
- **R3 — Performance:** first meaningful paint under 1.5s on a mid-tier laptop; the usage table
  must stay smooth above 10k rows (MERCURY-302).
- **R4 — Accessibility:** charts must meet WCAG AA contrast in both themes (MERCURY-303).
- **R5 — Resilience:** if the reports API is slow, the dashboard shows cached data with a
  staleness badge instead of a spinner.

## Out of scope

Billing transactions, invoice download, and write operations of any kind.

## Success metrics

Monthly active dashboards, ticket volume tagged "missing usage", and time-to-first-report after
signup. Target: 300 active dashboards and 60% ticket reduction by end of Q4 2026.

## Dependencies

Atlas reports API contract (MERCURY-304, resolved), Orion role claims (ORION-401).

doc_nova_guardrails.title: Nova Prompting and Grounding Guide
doc_nova_guardrails.content:
# Nova Prompting and Grounding Guide

**Owner:** Priya Sharma · **Related:** NOVA-203, NOVA-207, ADR-023

## Principle

Nova is a grounding system first and a language model second. The model is allowed to phrase an
answer; it is not allowed to originate a fact.

## Evidence contract

Every answer is assembled from an evidence bundle:

- **Graph facts** — parameterised traversals that produced nodes and relationships.
- **Document passages** — chunks retrieved from graph-linked documents, then vector-ranked.
- **Tickets and meetings** — operational context, always cited.

If the evidence bundle is empty, Nova must respond that it found no supporting information and
return a confidence below 0.3. There is no "best guess" path.

## Prompt structure

1. System: role, refusal policy, and the instruction to cite only supplied sources.
2. Context: the evidence bundle, each item tagged with a citation key.
3. Question: the user's question with resolved entities.
4. Output contract: a short answer, a list of citation keys used, and a confidence value.

## Confidence

Confidence combines source count, source type weight (decision and design documents weigh more than
tickets), and traversal depth. It is a communication aid, not a calibrated probability.

## Actions

The model may propose an action, never perform one. Proposals are rendered as a preview with the
target entity, the field values and a confirm control. Server-side code validates the proposal
against the whitelist before executing anything.

## Evaluation

A golden set of 40 questions with expected graph paths runs on every prompt change. A change that
lowers path accuracy below 95% blocks merge.

doc_nova_design.title: Nova Knowledge Assistant — System Design
doc_nova_design.content:
# Nova Knowledge Assistant — System Design

## Goal

Nova answers employee questions about people, projects, systems, documents and decisions — with
sources — by walking the company knowledge graph instead of relying on vector similarity alone.

## Why a graph first

Questions like "Who owns Project Atlas?" and "Why did we choose PostgreSQL?" are relationship
questions. Similarity search cannot traverse Person to OWNS to Project to HAS_DECISION to
Decision to SUPPORTED_BY to Document. Per ADR-015 the company graph lives in FalkorDB and every
factual answer must be reachable through a Cypher traversal plus document evidence.

## Pipeline

The workflow is a LangGraph state graph (ADR-023) with five agents:

1. **Intent agent** — classifies the request (person, project, decision, expertise, document,
   action, general) and extracts entities.
2. **Graph intelligence agent** — resolves entities to graph nodes and runs parameterised
   traversals. Arbitrary Cypher is never accepted from users; only whitelisted query templates.
3. **Knowledge retrieval agent** — hybrid retrieval: graph-linked documents first, then vector
   similarity over chunks for long-form detail.
4. **Reasoning agent** — composes the answer from evidence only, attaches sources and a graph
   path, and scores confidence. No evidence, no claim.
5. **Action agent** — proposes write actions (create ticket, assign task, schedule meeting) as a
   preview that requires explicit human confirmation before execution.

## Data model

Nodes: Person, Team, Project, Document, Decision, Ticket, Meeting, Technology, System, Skill,
Department. Relationships include MEMBER_OF, OWNS, WORKS_ON, KNOWS, EXPERT_IN, AUTHORED,
PARTICIPATED_IN, HAS_DOCUMENT, HAS_TICKET, HAS_DECISION, MADE_BY, ABOUT, SUPPORTED_BY,
DISCUSSED_IN, RELATED_TO, REFERENCES, USES and PART_OF.

## Embeddings and chunking

Documents are chunked by heading-aware paragraphs and embedded for hybrid retrieval. The graph
always supplies relationships; embeddings only supply passage-level detail.

## Failure behaviour

DEMO_MODE keeps the assistant usable without an LLM key: answers are composed deterministically
from live graph results. FalkorDB unavailability degrades to a clear service message rather than
a stack trace.

doc_orion_requirements.title: Orion Identity & Billing Requirements
doc_orion_requirements.content:
# Orion — Identity & Billing Requirements

**Owner:** Ananya Iyer (security) · **Product lead:** Sarah Thomas · **Status:** Planning

## Problem

Authentication is implemented three times: the legacy session service, the Mercury frontend
session cookie, and a partial SSO bridge. Logout behaviour differs across all three, and the Q3
access review could not reconstruct a complete audit trail. Billing is calculated from a nightly
batch with no event-level lineage.

## Goals

1. One identity gateway for all products, enforcing OIDC, MFA and RBAC (ADR-025, proposed).
2. Event-level billing with lineage back to Atlas usage events.
3. Complete audit trail: who acted, on what, under which policy.

## Requirements

- **R1 — OIDC:** authorization code flow with PKCE, JWKS rotation every 30 days (ORION-403).
- **R2 — MFA:** hardware-backed for production access, TOTP for customers.
- **R3 — RBAC:** role claims consumed by Mercury for report gating (MERCURY-301).
- **R4 — Billing events:** schema agreed with Atlas ingestion (ORION-402); every billed unit maps
  to a usage event ID.
- **R5 — Logout:** single gateway-mediated logout across all products (ORION-404, blocked on
  ADR-025).
- **R6 — Audit:** every token issue, refresh and revoke is written to the audit log with actor and
  purpose.

## Non-goals

Social login, SAML for enterprise customers, and anything that changes the Atlas data model.

## Risks

ADR-025 is still proposed; ORION-404 is blocked until it is approved. Migration of live sessions
needs a dual-run window to avoid forcing every user to reauthenticate at once.

## Success metrics

Zero divergent logout reports, 100% audit coverage of token lifecycle events, MFA adoption above
95% for internal users.

doc_platform_runbook.title: Platform Runbook
doc_platform_runbook.content:
# Platform Runbook

**Owner:** Vikram Raj · **Platform:** AWS EKS, GitHub Actions, Redis, PostgreSQL RDS

## Deployments

All production deployments go through GitHub Actions with GitOps (ADR-021). A deploy that bypasses
the pipeline is an incident. Rollback is `git revert` plus sync; median rollback time is 4 minutes.

## Cluster operations

- Node groups: `general` (m5.large) and `ai` (g5.xlarge, tainted for AI Services).
- Autoscaling targets CPU 65% / memory 70%. Cluster autoscaler adds nodes within 90 seconds.
- PodDisruptionBudgets are required for anything with more than one replica.

## Database operations

- RDS PostgreSQL 16, multi-AZ, 15-minute automated backups, 7-day PITR window.
- Read replica lag alerts at 30 seconds; page at 120 seconds.
- PgBouncer front-ends all application connections. Pool exhaustion near 600 RPS is tracked by
  ATLAS-109.

## Cache operations

Redis runs as a two-shard cluster with 6GB maxmemory and `allkeys-lru`. Memory pressure above 85%
for five minutes pages the on-call engineer. A cache redesign in September caused AI gateway p99
regression (NOVA-205) from eviction churn; the fix is a dedicated namespace per workload.

## Observability

- Dashboards: service RED metrics, database health, cache pressure, cost.
- Alerts route to the on-call rotation with severity in the page title.
- Every service logs correlation IDs; trace sampling is 10% steady, 100% during incidents.

## On-call

Seven-day rotations, handover notes required, and a blameless postmortem within five business days
for severity 1 or 2 incidents.

doc_security_policy.title: NovaTech Security Policy v2.1
doc_security_policy.content:
# NovaTech Security Policy v2.1

**Owner:** Ananya Iyer, Security Engineering
**Scope:** All product and internal systems

## Access control

All human access to production requires SSO with hardware-backed MFA. Access reviews run
quarterly; the Q3 review closed 14 of 16 findings. Per ADR-025 (proposed) all product sessions
move behind an Orion-managed OIDC gateway so that MFA, RBAC and audit logging are enforced in one
place rather than three.

## Data protection

Customer PII is encrypted at rest and in transit. Every read of customer data must be attributable
to an actor and a purpose (ATLAS-110). Secrets live in AWS Secrets Manager; committing a secret to
a repository is treated as a security incident.

## AI systems

Nova may not send customer PII to third-party model providers. Model calls are logged with prompt
hash, model identifier and token counts. Any AI feature that writes to company systems must
present a preview and receive explicit human confirmation (ADR-023, NOVA-207). Ungrounded answers
must be refused or returned with reduced confidence.

## Incident response

Severity 1 incidents page the on-call engineer within five minutes and require a written
postmortem within five business days. Postmortems are blameless and focus on system causes.

## Application security

Dependency scanning and SAST run on every pull request. High findings block merge. Threat modelling
is required for new external interfaces and for anything that changes authentication or
authorization behaviour.

## Review cadence

The policy is reviewed every six months or after any severity 1 security incident.

chunks.text:
**Author:** Ananya Iyer · **Scope:** Production systems, repositories, cloud accounts
**Cadence:** Quarterly (Security Policy v2.1)

Reviewed every human principal with production access against their current team and project

The index is reviewed monthly. If a decision's context changes materially, a superseding ADR is
written rather than editing history.
chunks.heading: Review

chunks.text:
Base URL: `https://atlas.novatech.example/api/v2`

All endpoints require a bearer token issued by the Auth Gateway and an `X-Purpose` header
describing the business purpose of the request (required for PII audit logging per ATLAS-110).
chunks.heading: Atlas Reports API

chunks.text:
Returns usage aggregates for the caller's tenant.

**Query parameters**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `from` | date | Inclusive period start |
| `to` | date | Inclusive period end |
| `plan` | string | Optional plan filter |
| `region` | string | Optional region filter |
| `group_by` | string | `day`, `week` or `month` |

**Response**

```json
{
  "tenant_id": "t_8421",
  "period": {"from": "2026-09-01", "to": "2026-09-30"},
  "reports": [
    {"bucket": "2026-09-01", "sum": 18402, "unit": "api_calls", "plan": "scale"}
  ],
  "staleness_seconds": 42
}
```

The response is served from the read replica; `staleness_seconds` tells the client how far behind
the replica is so the UI can show a freshness badge.
chunks.heading: GET /reports/usage

chunks.text:
Returns the customer record with plan and region. Sensitive fields are redacted unless the caller
carries the `customer:pii` scope.
chunks.heading: GET /customers/{id}

chunks.text:
| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 401 | Missing or invalid token |
| 403 | Missing scope |
| 409 | Schema version mismatch (see ATLAS-107) |
| 429 | Rate limited, retry after `Retry-After` |
| 503 | Replica unavailable, retry with backoff |
chunks.heading: Error codes

chunks.text:
Mercury consumes `/reports/usage` and must tolerate `staleness_seconds` up to 120 before alerting.
The `sum` field name is stable since v2.8 (contract drift fixed under MERCURY-304).
chunks.heading: Notes for consumers

chunks.text:
This document is the supporting design for ADR-018, which moved Atlas from MongoDB to PostgreSQL.

Three forces drove the migration:

1. **Consistency.** Reporting aggregates built in application code disagreed with operational
   counts under concurrent writes. MongoDB multi-document transactions existed but were slow and
   rarely used by the legacy repository layer.
2. **Join cost.** Cohort reporting needs joins across customers, plans and usage. Stitching in
   application code made every report a bespoke query.
3. **Cost.** Managed MongoDB spend grew 3.4x year over year while our Postgres footprint stayed flat.
chunks.heading: Problem statement

chunks.text:
PostgreSQL 16 on AWS RDS with multi-AZ. Monthly partitioned `usage_events`, encrypted PII columns,
PgBouncer for pooling, and a read replica for reporting (ADR-020).
chunks.heading: Target design

chunks.text:
Three phases:

- **Phase 1 — Dual write.** Writes go to MongoDB first, then PostgreSQL, with divergence logging (ATLAS-101).
- **Phase 2 — Shadow reads.** Reads still served by MongoDB while PostgreSQL responses are compared (ATLAS-101).
- **Phase 3 — Cutover and decommission.** Reads flip to PostgreSQL, then MongoDB is retired (ATLAS-106).

Backfill runs in resumable 50k-row chunks to keep replica lag under two seconds (ATLAS-102).
Index tuning for customer-by-region and customer-by-plan lookups landed in ATLAS-104.
chunks.heading: Migration strategy

chunks.text:
If divergence exceeds 0.1% of sampled queries, reads revert to MongoDB for one release cycle.

Reviewed with Priya Sharma and Meera Krishnan, approved by David Wilson in the Database
Architecture Review meeting on 2026-08-12 (ADR-018).
chunks.heading: Decision context

chunks.text:
**Author:** Meera Krishnan · **Owner:** Arun Kumar · **Related:** ADR-018, ATLAS-102, ATLAS-107

The ingestion pipeline turns raw product API events into the canonical `usage_events` table that
powers reporting and billing.
chunks.heading: Overview

chunks.text:
1. **Collect.** FastAPI ingest endpoints accept batched events, validate against the event schema
   and write to a Redis stream.
2. **Normalise.** Workers consume the stream, coerce types, resolve tenant and plan identifiers,
   and emit normalised rows.
3. **Load.** Rows are written to PostgreSQL in 5k-row transactions with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`
   for idempotency.
4. **Aggregate.** Hourly materialised views roll usage up by tenant, plan and region.
chunks.heading: Stages

chunks.text:
Historical backfill from MongoDB runs in resumable 50k-row chunks with checkpoints in Redis. Chunk
size was chosen so replica lag stays under two seconds, which is the threshold the reporting
staleness badge tolerates (ATLAS-102).
chunks.heading: Backfill

chunks.text:
- Event schema version is enforced at ingest; unknown versions are rejected with a metric.
- A nightly reconciliation job compares hourly aggregates against raw counts and alerts on
  divergence above 0.05%.
- Contract tests compare ingest output to the API model, added after ATLAS-107 found a
  `plan_tier` vs `planTier` mismatch.
chunks.heading: Data quality

chunks.text:
| Failure | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Redis stream full | Ingest sheds load with 429 and a retry hint |
| Postgres primary failover | Workers retry with exponential backoff, stream retains events |
| Schema drift | Rows quarantined to `usage_events_quarantine` and alerted |
chunks.heading: Failure modes

chunks.text: Cold-data archival to S3 (ATLAS-108) and a schema registry to remove the manual contract tests.
chunks.heading: Open work

chunks.text:
**Overall health:** At risk (yellow)
**Owner:** Arun Kumar · **Lead:** David Wilson · **Product:** Sarah Thomas

The PostgreSQL migration is functionally complete for new writes and backfill is 92% done. The
project is flagged at risk for schedule, not for correctness: reporting latency and connection
pooling both need work before we can decommission MongoDB.
chunks.heading: Summary

chunks.text:
- ADR-018 approved and implemented for primary workloads.
- ADR-020 approved: read replica added for reporting.
- ATLAS-102 backfill at 92% of historical usage events.
- ATLAS-104 index tuning closed with a 6x improvement on customer lookups.
chunks.heading: Progress this quarter

chunks.text:
1. **Connection pool exhaustion (ATLAS-109).** PgBouncer saturates at 600 RPS in load tests.
   Mitigation under investigation by Arun with Vikram's load harness.
2. **Reporting latency (ATLAS-105).** Dashboard p95 hit 2.8s during ingest peaks. The read replica
   work moves reporting off the primary.
3. **Schema drift (ATLAS-107).** Ingest and API disagree on `planTier` casing; a contract test is
   being added.
chunks.heading: Risks

chunks.text:
- Finish backfill and shadow-read validation, then retire MongoDB (ATLAS-106).
- Complete audit logging for PII reads (ATLAS-110) ahead of the security review.
- Hand stable reporting views to the Mercury beta.
chunks.heading: Next quarter

chunks.text:
Infrastructure spend is down 19% quarter over quarter, driven by the MongoDB reduction. No new
headcount requested.
chunks.heading: Budget note

chunks.text:
Atlas is NovaTech's customer data platform. It ingests product usage events, joins them with
customer records, and serves analytics to the Mercury dashboard and the Nova knowledge pipeline.
chunks.heading: Overview

chunks.text:
Ingestion workers consume events from the product APIs and write them through a FastAPI ingest
service. Since ADR-018 the system of record is PostgreSQL on AWS RDS, with MongoDB retained only
as a shadow source during the cutover window. Reporting queries run against a PostgreSQL read
replica as approved in ADR-020.

Redis provides the result cache for dashboard aggregates and the durable queue for background
ingest jobs. All services run as containers on AWS EKS (ADR-021) and are deployed through GitHub
Actions pipelines with required checks on main.
chunks.heading: Current topology

chunks.text:
Three tables carry most of the load: `customers`, `usage_events` and `plans`. Usage events are
append-only and partitioned monthly. Customer PII columns are encrypted at rest and every read is
audit logged per ATLAS-110.
chunks.heading: Data model core

chunks.text:
The reporting use cases are dominated by joins between customers, plans and usage aggregates.
Application-side stitching in the MongoDB era produced inconsistent aggregates and cost 3.4x more
to operate. PostgreSQL gives transactional consistency, window functions for cohort queries, and a
single operational model shared with Orion and Nova.
chunks.heading: Why relational

chunks.text:
- Connection pooling saturates near 600 RPS (ATLAS-109).
- Reporting latency regressed during write peaks, tracked by ADR-020 and ATLAS-105.
- Dual-write divergence checks are still running (ATLAS-101).
chunks.heading: Known pressure points

chunks.text:
Arun Kumar is the technical owner. Meera Krishnan owns the ingestion pipeline. David Wilson
approved the architecture. Sarah Thomas owns the product-facing reporting commitments.
chunks.heading: Owners

chunks.text:
**Owner:** Rahul Menon · **Consumers:** Mercury, Nova dashboard, internal tools

1. **Information before decoration.** Every pixel either carries meaning or gets removed.
2. **Dark first.** The default theme is dark; light mode is a supported alternative, not an
   afterthought.
3. **Motion with purpose.** Transitions explain state changes, never entertain.
chunks.heading: Principles

chunks.text:
- **Colour:** deep slate surfaces (`#0f1218`, `#161b24`), one accent (cyan `#38bdf8`), semantic
  colours for success, warning and danger. Contrast checked against WCAG AA in both themes.
- **Typography:** system UI stack for product pages; monospace for identifiers, ticket keys and
  code. Numeric data uses tabular figures.
- **Spacing:** 4px base scale. Cards use 16px padding, 12px gaps.
- **Elevation:** two levels only — resting and raised. Raised surfaces get a 1px border plus a soft
  shadow; we avoid large blur radii.
chunks.heading: Foundations

chunks.text:
Buttons (primary, ghost, danger), inputs with inline validation, cards, badges for status
(`healthy`, `degraded`, `blocked`), and a data table with virtualised rows. Status colours are
always paired with a text label; colour alone never conveys state.
chunks.heading: Components

chunks.text:
Axis and grid lines at 12% opacity. Legends use the accessibility palette and sit above the chart
on narrow viewports. Tooltips show exact values, never rounded ones.
chunks.heading: Charts

chunks.text:
Keyboard reachable controls, visible focus rings, `prefers-reduced-motion` respected. Icons that
carry meaning have text labels.
chunks.heading: Accessibility

chunks.text:
Tokens ship as CSS custom properties plus a TypeScript object. Components are themed by token, never
by conditional classes. New components require a story and an axe check before merge.
chunks.heading: Implementation notes

chunks.text:
These guidelines are the default for every repository. Deviations require an ADR.

- **Backend:** Python 3.12 with FastAPI (ADR-009). Typed Pydantic request/response models and a
  generated OpenAPI schema are mandatory for every service.
- **Frontend:** React with Vite and TypeScript (ADR-012). Shared components live in the internal
  design system.
- **Ephemeral state:** Redis for caches, sessions and queues (ADR-006).
- **Graph and relationship data:** FalkorDB with parameterised Cypher (ADR-015).
chunks.heading: Language and framework defaults

chunks.text:
PostgreSQL is the system of record (ADR-018). Schema changes ship as versioned migrations and are
reviewed by a second engineer. No service writes to another service's tables; use its API.
chunks.heading: Data

chunks.text:
- Trunk-based development, short-lived branches, required checks on main (ADR-017).
- Every change to production infrastructure goes through GitOps; no manual deploys (ADR-021).
- Tests required for new behaviour: unit tests for logic, API tests for endpoints, an integration
  test for anything touching two services.
chunks.heading: Delivery

chunks.text:
Structured JSON logs with correlation IDs, RED metrics for every service, and dashboards that
answer "is the customer affected" before "which box is hot".
chunks.heading: Observability

chunks.text:
Reviewers check for: typed interfaces at boundaries, explicit error handling, no secrets in the
repo, and documentation for any non-obvious decision. Reviews are about the code, never the
person who wrote it.
chunks.heading: Code review

chunks.text:
Any AI feature must (1) cite its sources, (2) degrade gracefully when a model provider is
unavailable, and (3) require human confirmation before performing write actions. Prompt and
evaluation changes are reviewed like code.
chunks.heading: AI features

chunks.text:
Welcome to NovaTech. This handbook gets you from laptop to first pull request in a day.

1. **Accounts.** SSO through the identity provider, then ask your team lead for repository access.
2. **Local environment.** Docker Desktop, Python 3.12, Node 20, and `uv` or `poetry`. Every service
   has a `docker compose` file that boots it with dependencies.
3. **Read these first.** Engineering Guidelines v3, the Security Policy, and the architecture
   document for the project you joined.
chunks.heading: Week one

chunks.text:
We develop in trunk-based style with short-lived branches and required checks on main. Every
change needs one review. We use ADRs for decisions that are expensive to reverse: if you are
choosing a database, an auth model, or a deployment platform, write an ADR.
chunks.heading: How we work

chunks.text:
- Backend, data platform, database migrations: **Arun Kumar**
- AI platform, agent orchestration, retrieval quality: **Priya Sharma**
- Frontend, design system, performance: **Rahul Menon**
- Kubernetes, CI/CD, cloud cost: **Vikram Raj**
- Security reviews, threat modelling, access: **Ananya Iyer**
- Data pipelines and warehouse modelling: **Meera Krishnan**
- Roadmap, priorities, customer context: **Sarah Thomas**
- Architecture escalations: **David Wilson**
chunks.heading: Who to ask

chunks.text:
Pick a "good first issue" from your team's backlog. Your mentor reviews it with you. Team leads own
the backlog grooming, so ask them if the issue is unclear.
chunks.heading: Your first task

chunks.text:
Documents, decisions and meeting notes are indexed in the company knowledge graph. Ask Nova in the
dashboard: it answers with sources, and walking the virtual office to a desk or room gives you the
same graph with context.
chunks.heading: Where knowledge lives

chunks.text:
**Severity:** 2 · **Duration:** 74 minutes · **Author:** Vikram Raj

A production deploy of the Atlas ingest service left the fleet in a mixed state: six of nine EC2
instances ran the new build while three kept the old one. Ingest throughput dropped 40% and
duplicate usage rows appeared for 11 minutes.
chunks.heading: Summary

chunks.text:
- 14:02 — Deploy command issued by hand over SSH to the instance list.
- 14:05 — Three instances rejected the artifact due to a checksum mismatch.
- 14:09 — Mixed-version fleet caused duplicate writes for tenants on both versions.
- 15:16 — Fleet rolled back to the previous artifact; duplication stopped.
chunks.heading: Timeline

chunks.text:
Deploys were a hand-rolled script over a hard-coded instance list with no atomicity, no
verification and no rollback path. The checksum mismatch was a symptom; the absence of a release
mechanism was the cause.
chunks.heading: Root cause

chunks.text:
11 minutes of duplicate usage rows (since deduplicated), 40% ingest degradation for 74 minutes, no
customer data loss.

- No staging environment matched production at the time.
- Artifact checksums were computed per host rather than centrally.
chunks.heading: Contributing factors

chunks.text:
1. Approved ADR-021: move production to AWS EKS with GitOps deployments (approved 2026-07-09).
2. Added artifact checksum verification to the release pipeline.
3. Staging cluster raised to production parity in node count.
chunks.heading: Actions taken

chunks.text:
Deployment is a system, not a command. Standardise the platform before optimising the process.
This incident is the primary evidence behind ADR-021.
chunks.heading: Lessons

chunks.text:
**Severity:** 3 · **Duration:** 6 days (regression, not outage) · **Author:** Vikram Raj

After the September cache redesign, AI Services p99 latency rose from 1.9s to 4.7s. No requests
failed, but interactive Nova sessions felt sluggish and the team's own usage dropped.
chunks.heading: Summary

chunks.text:
- Sep 16 — Cache redesign deployed, moving all workloads onto one Redis keyspace.
- Sep 18 — AI gateway p99 crosses 3s; alert threshold not yet breached.
- Sep 22 — Weekly incident triage (meet_012) confirms the correlation.
- Sep 26 — Dedicated Redis namespace for AI workloads restores p99 to 2.0s.
chunks.heading: Timeline

chunks.text:
The shared Redis keyspace let high-churn report caches evict the AI gateway's prompt-cache entries
under `allkeys-lru`. Eviction churn increased upstream model calls, which dominate latency.
chunks.heading: Root cause

chunks.text:
Elevated latency for six days. No data loss, no failed requests, no customer-visible errors.

- Dedicated Redis namespace per workload class.
- Cache hit ratio dashboard added; alert at below 60% for AI workloads.
- NOVA-205 tracks the permanent fix and verification.
chunks.heading: Actions taken

chunks.text:
Caching is a shared resource with a fairness problem. Per-workload isolation should have been part
of the cache redesign review. Triage cadence caught this, but two days later than an alert would
have.
chunks.heading: Lessons

chunks.text:
**Attendees:** Arun Kumar, Priya Sharma, David Wilson, Meera Krishnan
**Outcome:** ADR-018 approved

1. MongoDB to PostgreSQL migration proposal for Atlas
2. Reporting join strategy
3. Cutover phasing and rollback criteria
chunks.heading: Agenda

chunks.text:
Arun presented the cost and consistency analysis: MongoDB spend had grown 3.4x year over year,
and reporting aggregates built in application code disagreed with operational counts under
concurrent writes. Meera showed that cohort reporting requires joins across customers, plans and
usage events, which the document store could not express efficiently.

Priya confirmed that Nova ingestion also needs relational guarantees: the knowledge graph seed
pipeline reads canonical project and decision data, and inconsistent aggregates would poison
retrieval quality. She supported PostgreSQL as the system of record.

David asked about rollback. Arun described the three-phase plan with divergence logging at 0.1%
threshold from the migration design document. David approved ADR-018 with that rollback clause.
chunks.heading: Discussion

chunks.text:
- **ADR-018 approved:** move Atlas from MongoDB to PostgreSQL on AWS RDS.
- Dual-write shadow reads proceed under ATLAS-101.
- Backfill sized at 50k-row resumable chunks (ATLAS-102).
chunks.heading: Decisions

chunks.text:
| Action | Owner | Due |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dual-write divergence logging | Arun Kumar | 2026-08-22 |
| Backfill scripts with checkpoints | Meera Krishnan | 2026-08-29 |
| Reporting view rewrite | Arun Kumar | 2026-09-12 |
chunks.heading: Actions

chunks.text:
**Author:** Rahul Menon · **Stack:** React 18, Vite, TypeScript (ADR-012)

Feature-sliced layout: `features/reports`, `features/account`, `features/shared`. Each feature owns
its components, hooks and API client. Cross-feature imports go through the shared design system,
never sideways into another feature.
chunks.heading: Structure

chunks.text:
A thin typed client wraps the Atlas Reports API. Response types are generated from the OpenAPI
schema so contract drift fails at compile time — the same class of bug as MERCURY-304 but caught in
CI instead of production.

Caching uses stale-while-revalidate: the dashboard renders cached data with a freshness badge while
refetching. The freshness badge reads `staleness_seconds` from the API, tolerating up to 120s before
warning.
chunks.heading: Data layer

chunks.text:
The usage table is windowed and virtualised (MERCURY-302). Above 10k rows we render only visible
rows plus a 20-row overscan; sorting and filtering are memoised over a normalised index.

Charts render to canvas with a shared theme object. Legend colours come from the accessibility-safe
palette; ADR for dark mode contrast is tracked in MERCURY-303.
chunks.heading: Rendering performance

chunks.text:
Server state lives in the query cache; UI state lives in local component state. There is no global
store, deliberately: the dashboard has no cross-feature client state worth centralising.
chunks.heading: State

chunks.text:
Vitest for units, Playwright for the three critical journeys (login, view report, export CSV).
Accessibility checked with axe on every component story.
chunks.heading: Testing

chunks.text:
Charts re-render on window resize without debounce, and the export path duplicates formatting
logic that lives in the shared package.
chunks.heading: Known debt

chunks.text:
**Owner:** Sarah Thomas · **Engineering owner:** Rahul Menon · **Status:** In development

Customers see their NovaTech usage only through monthly emailed PDFs. Support tickets about
"missing usage" average 40 per month, and the top churn reason in exit interviews is "we cannot
see what we are paying for".
chunks.heading: Problem

chunks.text:
1. Give customers a self-serve, role-aware usage dashboard.
2. Cut "missing usage" tickets by 60% within two quarters.
3. Ship on the standard React, Vite and TypeScript stack (ADR-012).
chunks.heading: Goals

chunks.text:
- **R1 — Reports:** usage by plan, region and period with CSV export. Data from the Atlas reports
  API, served from the PostgreSQL read replica (ADR-020).
- **R2 — Roles:** report tabs are gated by the Orion role claim; the frontend must not decide
  authorization on its own.
- **R3 — Performance:** first meaningful paint under 1.5s on a mid-tier laptop; the usage table
  must stay smooth above 10k rows (MERCURY-302).
- **R4 — Accessibility:** charts must meet WCAG AA contrast in both themes (MERCURY-303).
- **R5 — Resilience:** if the reports API is slow, the dashboard shows cached data with a
  staleness badge instead of a spinner.
chunks.heading: Requirements

chunks.text:
Billing transactions, invoice download, and write operations of any kind.

Monthly active dashboards, ticket volume tagged "missing usage", and time-to-first-report after
signup. Target: 300 active dashboards and 60% ticket reduction by end of Q4 2026.
chunks.heading: Success metrics

chunks.text: Atlas reports API contract (MERCURY-304, resolved), Orion role claims (ORION-401).
chunks.heading: Dependencies

chunks.text:
**Owner:** Priya Sharma · **Related:** NOVA-203, NOVA-207, ADR-023

Nova is a grounding system first and a language model second. The model is allowed to phrase an
answer; it is not allowed to originate a fact.
chunks.heading: Principle

chunks.text:
Every answer is assembled from an evidence bundle:

- **Graph facts** — parameterised traversals that produced nodes and relationships.
- **Document passages** — chunks retrieved from graph-linked documents, then vector-ranked.
- **Tickets and meetings** — operational context, always cited.

If the evidence bundle is empty, Nova must respond that it found no supporting information and
return a confidence below 0.3. There is no "best guess" path.
chunks.heading: Evidence contract

chunks.text:
1. System: role, refusal policy, and the instruction to cite only supplied sources.
2. Context: the evidence bundle, each item tagged with a citation key.
3. Question: the user's question with resolved entities.
4. Output contract: a short answer, a list of citation keys used, and a confidence value.
chunks.heading: Prompt structure

chunks.text:
Confidence combines source count, source type weight (decision and design documents weigh more than
tickets), and traversal depth. It is a communication aid, not a calibrated probability.
chunks.heading: Confidence

chunks.text:
The model may propose an action, never perform one. Proposals are rendered as a preview with the
target entity, the field values and a confirm control. Server-side code validates the proposal
against the whitelist before executing anything.
chunks.heading: Actions

chunks.text:
A golden set of 40 questions with expected graph paths runs on every prompt change. A change that
lowers path accuracy below 95% blocks merge.
chunks.heading: Evaluation

chunks.text:
Nova answers employee questions about people, projects, systems, documents and decisions — with
sources — by walking the company knowledge graph instead of relying on vector similarity alone.
chunks.heading: Goal

chunks.text:
Questions like "Who owns Project Atlas?" and "Why did we choose PostgreSQL?" are relationship
questions. Similarity search cannot traverse Person to OWNS to Project to HAS_DECISION to
Decision to SUPPORTED_BY to Document. Per ADR-015 the company graph lives in FalkorDB and every
factual answer must be reachable through a Cypher traversal plus document evidence.
chunks.heading: Why a graph first

chunks.text:
The workflow is a LangGraph state graph (ADR-023) with five agents:

1. **Intent agent** — classifies the request (person, project, decision, expertise, document,
   action, general) and extracts entities.
2. **Graph intelligence agent** — resolves entities to graph nodes and runs parameterised
   traversals. Arbitrary Cypher is never accepted from users; only whitelisted query templates.
3. **Knowledge retrieval agent** — hybrid retrieval: graph-linked documents first, then vector
   similarity over chunks for long-form detail.
4. **Reasoning agent** — composes the answer from evidence only, attaches sources and a graph
   path, and scores confidence. No evidence, no claim.
5. **Action agent** — proposes write actions (create ticket, assign task, schedule meeting) as a
   preview that requires explicit human confirmation before execution.
chunks.heading: Pipeline

chunks.text:
Nodes: Person, Team, Project, Document, Decision, Ticket, Meeting, Technology, System, Skill,
Department. Relationships include MEMBER_OF, OWNS, WORKS_ON, KNOWS, EXPERT_IN, AUTHORED,
PARTICIPATED_IN, HAS_DOCUMENT, HAS_TICKET, HAS_DECISION, MADE_BY, ABOUT, SUPPORTED_BY,
DISCUSSED_IN, RELATED_TO, REFERENCES, USES and PART_OF.
chunks.heading: Data model

chunks.text:
Documents are chunked by heading-aware paragraphs and embedded for hybrid retrieval. The graph
always supplies relationships; embeddings only supply passage-level detail.
chunks.heading: Embeddings and chunking

chunks.text:
DEMO_MODE keeps the assistant usable without an LLM key: answers are composed deterministically
from live graph results. FalkorDB unavailability degrades to a clear service message rather than
a stack trace.
chunks.heading: Failure behaviour

chunks.text:
**Owner:** Ananya Iyer (security) · **Product lead:** Sarah Thomas · **Status:** Planning

Authentication is implemented three times: the legacy session service, the Mercury frontend
session cookie, and a partial SSO bridge. Logout behaviour differs across all three, and the Q3
access review could not reconstruct a complete audit trail. Billing is calculated from a nightly
batch with no event-level lineage.
chunks.heading: Problem

chunks.text:
1. One identity gateway for all products, enforcing OIDC, MFA and RBAC (ADR-025, proposed).
2. Event-level billing with lineage back to Atlas usage events.
3. Complete audit trail: who acted, on what, under which policy.
chunks.heading: Goals

chunks.text:
- **R1 — OIDC:** authorization code flow with PKCE, JWKS rotation every 30 days (ORION-403).
- **R2 — MFA:** hardware-backed for production access, TOTP for customers.
- **R3 — RBAC:** role claims consumed by Mercury for report gating (MERCURY-301).
- **R4 — Billing events:** schema agreed with Atlas ingestion (ORION-402); every billed unit maps
  to a usage event ID.
- **R5 — Logout:** single gateway-mediated logout across all products (ORION-404, blocked on
  ADR-025).
- **R6 — Audit:** every token issue, refresh and revoke is written to the audit log with actor and
  purpose.
chunks.heading: Requirements

chunks.text:
Social login, SAML for enterprise customers, and anything that changes the Atlas data model.

ADR-025 is still proposed; ORION-404 is blocked until it is approved. Migration of live sessions
needs a dual-run window to avoid forcing every user to reauthenticate at once.
chunks.heading: Risks

chunks.text:
Zero divergent logout reports, 100% audit coverage of token lifecycle events, MFA adoption above
95% for internal users.
chunks.heading: Success metrics

chunks.text:
**Owner:** Vikram Raj · **Platform:** AWS EKS, GitHub Actions, Redis, PostgreSQL RDS

All production deployments go through GitHub Actions with GitOps (ADR-021). A deploy that bypasses
the pipeline is an incident. Rollback is `git revert` plus sync; median rollback time is 4 minutes.
chunks.heading: Deployments

chunks.text:
- Node groups: `general` (m5.large) and `ai` (g5.xlarge, tainted for AI Services).
- Autoscaling targets CPU 65% / memory 70%. Cluster autoscaler adds nodes within 90 seconds.
- PodDisruptionBudgets are required for anything with more than one replica.
chunks.heading: Cluster operations

chunks.text:
- RDS PostgreSQL 16, multi-AZ, 15-minute automated backups, 7-day PITR window.
- Read replica lag alerts at 30 seconds; page at 120 seconds.
- PgBouncer front-ends all application connections. Pool exhaustion near 600 RPS is tracked by
  ATLAS-109.
chunks.heading: Database operations

chunks.text:
Redis runs as a two-shard cluster with 6GB maxmemory and `allkeys-lru`. Memory pressure above 85%
for five minutes pages the on-call engineer. A cache redesign in September caused AI gateway p99
regression (NOVA-205) from eviction churn; the fix is a dedicated namespace per workload.
chunks.heading: Cache operations

chunks.text:
- Dashboards: service RED metrics, database health, cache pressure, cost.
- Alerts route to the on-call rotation with severity in the page title.
- Every service logs correlation IDs; trace sampling is 10% steady, 100% during incidents.
chunks.heading: Observability

chunks.text:
Seven-day rotations, handover notes required, and a blameless postmortem within five business days
for severity 1 or 2 incidents.
chunks.heading: On-call

chunks.text:
**Owner:** Ananya Iyer, Security Engineering
**Scope:** All product and internal systems

All human access to production requires SSO with hardware-backed MFA. Access reviews run
quarterly; the Q3 review closed 14 of 16 findings. Per ADR-025 (proposed) all product sessions
move behind an Orion-managed OIDC gateway so that MFA, RBAC and audit logging are enforced in one
place rather than three.
chunks.heading: Access control

chunks.text:
Customer PII is encrypted at rest and in transit. Every read of customer data must be attributable
to an actor and a purpose (ATLAS-110). Secrets live in AWS Secrets Manager; committing a secret to
a repository is treated as a security incident.
chunks.heading: Data protection

chunks.text:
Nova may not send customer PII to third-party model providers. Model calls are logged with prompt
hash, model identifier and token counts. Any AI feature that writes to company systems must
present a preview and receive explicit human confirmation (ADR-023, NOVA-207). Ungrounded answers
must be refused or returned with reduced confidence.
chunks.heading: AI systems

chunks.text:
Severity 1 incidents page the on-call engineer within five minutes and require a written
postmortem within five business days. Postmortems are blameless and focus on system causes.
chunks.heading: Incident response

chunks.text:
Dependency scanning and SAST run on every pull request. High findings block merge. Threat modelling
is required for new external interfaces and for anything that changes authentication or
authorization behaviour.
chunks.heading: Application security

chunks.text: The policy is reviewed every six months or after any severity 1 security incident.
chunks.heading: Review cadence
